terminal.description: A terminal in your workspace. `node ask.js server.js` starts your server, sends it each request in `requests.txt`, shows every answer and what the server printed, then stops it. `node server.js` runs it for a browser at http://localhost:3000 until you press Ctrl+C.

tasks.title: Answer every request with the free plots
tasks.description:
Write `server.js` so that it makes a server with `createServer` from `node:http` and listens on the port in the setting `PORT`. Once it is listening, it prints:

```
Listening on http://localhost:3000
```

with the port it listens on. Every request, whatever its address, gets the free plots of `plots.txt`, the file beside the script, as the body of the answer:

```
Free plots: A3, B2, C3.
```

or `No plots are free.` when there are none. Rhiannon edits `plots.txt` while the server runs, so read it each time a request comes.

Try it with `node ask.js server.js`. Check starts your server from another folder with a `PORT` and a `plots.txt` of its own, sends it requests to different addresses, and changes `plots.txt` between them.
nextSteps: Make the server with `createServer`, and give it a function that gets each request and its answer.
Read the port from `process.env.PORT` and call `listen` with it; print the line once listening.
In the function, read `plots.txt` from the script's folder and work out the free plots, as in the first part of this repo.
End the answer with the line as its body.
hints: A request waits until its answer is ended. Until then the browser, or `ask.js`, keeps waiting.
The function given to `createServer` gets `(req, res)`. `res.end(text)` sends `text` as the body and finishes the answer. It can be an `async` function, so it may `await readFile(...)`.
`const server = createServer(async (req, res) => { res.end(await freePlots()) })`, then `server.listen(process.env.PORT, () => console.log(...))`.

tasks.title: Say what kind of answer it is
tasks.description:
Change `server.js` so that the answer with the free plots has the status `200` and the header `Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8`, which tells a browser the body is plain text in UTF-8.

When `plots.txt` cannot be read, because Rhiannon is saving it or it is gone, the answer has the status `500` and the same header, and its body is:

```
The plot list cannot be read.
```

The server keeps running, and once the file is back the free plots are answered again.

Check sends requests, removes `plots.txt` and sends more, then puts a new one back.
nextSteps: Set the status and the header before the body is sent.
Remove `plots.txt` for a moment, run `node ask.js server.js`, and see what happens now.
Catch the error that reading the file throws, and answer with status 500 and the line from the task.
hints: An error thrown by an `await` that nobody catches ends the whole server, not only the one request.
`res.statusCode = 500` sets the status and `res.setHeader(name, value)` a header. Both have to come before the body: once part of it is sent, they have gone.
`res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/plain; charset=utf-8')`, then `try { res.end(await freePlots()) } catch { res.statusCode = 500; res.end('The plot list cannot be read.') }`.

tasks.title: Choose the port, and say when it is taken
tasks.description:
Change `server.js` so that:

- When `PORT` is not set, or is empty, it listens on `3000`.
- When `PORT` is not a whole number from 1 to 65535, such as `abc` or `80.5`, it prints one line on standard error that names `PORT`, nothing on standard output, does not listen, and ends with exit code 1.
- When the port is already in use by another program, it prints one line on standard error that names the port, such as `Port 3000 is already in use.`, and ends with exit code 1, without Node's error and its stack.

Try them with `node ask.js PORT=abc server.js` and `node ask.js --busy server.js`. Check starts your server with `PORT` not set, empty and set to ports that are not ports, and once with its port taken.
nextSteps: Use 3000 when the setting is missing or empty, as in the issue on settings.
Turn the setting into a number and refuse it when it is not a whole number from 1 to 65535, before listening.
Run `node ask.js --busy server.js` and read the error Node stops with.
Listen for the server's `error` event, and for `EADDRINUSE` print one line and set the exit code.
hints: A server that cannot listen does not throw where `listen` is called. It emits an `error` event a moment later, and with no listener for it, Node stops the script with the error.
`server.on('error', (error) => ...)` gets the error. Its `code` is `'EADDRINUSE'` when the port is taken. `Number.isInteger` is false for `NaN` and for `80.5`.
`server.on('error', (error) => { if (error.code === 'EADDRINUSE') console.error(`Port ${port} is already in use.`); process.exitCode = 1 })`.

tasks.title: Stop the server on Ctrl+C
tasks.description:
A server keeps running until someone stops it, and Ctrl+C ends it on the spot, in the middle of whatever it was sending. Change `server.js` so that Ctrl+C, the `SIGINT` signal, closes the server: it stops taking requests, lets the answers on their way finish, then prints:

```
Server stopped.
```

and the script ends by itself with exit code 0.

Check sends your server requests, then raises `SIGINT` inside it, the way Ctrl+C does, and waits for it to end by itself.
nextSteps: Run `node server.js`, press Ctrl+C, and see what is printed now.
Listen for `SIGINT` on `process`, as in the issue on timers.
In the listener, close the server, and print the line once it has closed.
Run it again and check the prompt comes back after Ctrl+C.
hints: A listening server keeps the script alive, like a timer. Until it is closed, the script does not end by itself.
`server.close(callback)` stops taking new requests and calls `callback` once the last answer is finished.
